<USER_REQUEST>
MASTER PROMPT — Trilogy “Promise Them Nothing Twice” Assignment
You are my senior software engineer, systems architect, debugging partner, and coding agent.
We are completing the Trilogy Technology Internship take-home assignment:
Repository:
[https://github.com/trilogy-group/ti-assignment-promise-them-nothin](https://github.com/trilogy-group/ti-assignment-promise-them-nothin)
The assignment is called “Promise Them Nothing Twice.”
Your job is to help me complete the assignment to a very high engineering standard while also producing a strong, honest, auditable AI-assisted development process.
CRITICAL WORKING RULE
DO NOT attempt to complete the entire assignment in one step.
We will work through the assignment in clearly separated phases.
After completing EACH phase:
Stop.
Tell me exactly what you did.
Tell me what files changed.
Tell me what you learned/discovered.
Tell me what decisions you made and why.
Tell me what you verified/tested.
Tell me about any uncertainty, weakness, assumption, or unresolved issue.
Give me a concise PHASE COMPLETE summary.
Then WAIT for my instruction before beginning the next phase.
Do not silently continue into the next phase.
I want to be able to use our complete conversation/session as part of the required AI-session export, so your work must be transparent and easy for a reviewer to follow.
OUR OBJECTIVE
Complete the assignment in a way that demonstrates strong engineering judgment rather than simply producing lots of code.
The final result should be:
Correct
Runnable locally
Easy for a reviewer to understand
Properly tested
Distributed in a realistic way
Honest about guarantees and limitations
Narrow rather than unnecessarily feature-heavy
Well documented
Supported by a convincing load-testing harness
Supported by a concise DECISIONS.md
Consistent with the assignment's stakeholder conflict
Easy to run on a laptop using free tools
Do NOT optimize for maximum feature count.
Optimize for:
correctness + reasoning + verification + clarity + engineering judgment.
IMPORTANT ASSIGNMENT CONTEXT
Before writing implementation code, inspect the repository and read ALL relevant assignment material.
At minimum inspect:
assignment.md
briefs/cto-memo.md
briefs/support-lead-memo.md
briefs/platform-context.md
submission/README.md
submission/DECISIONS.template.md
Any other relevant repository files
Do not assume that assignment.md is a complete cleaned-up specification. The conflicting stakeholder memos are intentionally part of the problem.
The central conflict must be explicitly resolved rather than hidden.
The assignment describes:
RelayAPI
Per-customer RPM quotas
Three stateless application nodes
A load balancer
No sticky-session requirement
Northwind Logistics as the largest customer
Conflicting CTO and Support requirements
The CTO requires strict quota enforcement, per-customer isolation, fairness, auditability, and distributed correctness.
The support lead wants Northwind to avoid 429 responses during its nightly batch window.
Do NOT simply implement both requirements as though they are simultaneously and literally satisfiable.
We must make an explicit engineering decision about the conflict and document what we accept and reject.
PHASE STRUCTURE
Follow this exact workflow unless we explicitly change it together.
PHASE 0 — Repository & Assignment Reconnaissance
First inspect the repository and assignment completely.
Do NOT implement anything.
Determine:
Exact assignment requirements
Deliverables
Submission structure
Stakeholder conflict
Technical constraints
Evaluation criteria
Required AI session artifacts
Existing templates
Expected behavior
Hidden traps or ambiguous areas
What the evaluator is likely to test
What the evaluator likely considers a weak solution
Also inspect the three stakeholder documents carefully.
At the end of this phase provide:
Phase 0 Report
1. What the assignment actually asks
2. Stakeholder conflict
3. Hard requirements
4. Soft/negotiable decisions
5. Technical risks
6. Likely failure modes
7. What a naive candidate would probably do wrong
8. What a strong submission should demonstrate
9. Proposed implementation phases
10. Questions/uncertainties that need resolution
DO NOT write implementation code yet.
WAIT.
PHASE 1 — Engineering Decision & Architecture
Based on Phase 0, design the solution before implementing it.
Compare reasonable rate-limiting approaches such as:
Fixed window
Sliding window
Token bucket
Leaky bucket
Hybrid approaches
Evaluate them specifically against:
Strict quota enforcement
Fairness
Burst behavior
Distributed coordination
Three stateless application nodes
Race conditions
Boundary behavior
Auditability
Simplicity
Laptop-friendly development
Correctness under concurrent requests
Do not choose an algorithm merely because it is popular.
Explain why the selected algorithm fits THIS assignment.
Then design:
Service architecture
Rate limiter architecture
Shared state mechanism
Customer identity model
Quota configuration
Request flow
Error behavior
429 behavior
Retry-After
Distributed coordination
Concurrency behavior
Node-to-node behavior
Failure behavior
Observability/auditability
Load harness architecture
Explicitly identify guarantees we CAN provide and guarantees we CANNOT provide.
Do not over-engineer.
At the end provide:
Phase 1 Report
Chosen architecture
Alternatives considered
Why alternatives were rejected
Chosen algorithm
Why it was chosen
Distributed-state design
Data model
Request lifecycle
Concurrency strategy
Expected boundary behavior
Known limitations
Proposed repository structure
WAIT.
PHASE 2 — Technology Selection & Project Skeleton
Choose the implementation language/framework/dependencies.
Prefer technologies that:
Are free
Are easy to install
Are commonly understood
Require minimal infrastructure
Can run locally
Make distributed behavior demonstrable
Are easy for a reviewer to run in under ~15 minutes
Before adding a dependency, justify why it is necessary.
Create the initial project structure.
Do NOT implement the complete rate limiter yet.
Set up:
Service skeleton
Configuration
Dependency management
Basic application startup
Health endpoint if appropriate
Test infrastructure
Initial README structure
Placeholder harness structure if appropriate
Then run the application and verify the skeleton actually works.
At the end report:
Files created
Dependencies added
Commands used
What successfully runs
What is still missing
Why each major structural decision was made
WAIT.
PHASE 3 — Implement the Core Rate Limiter
Now implement the smallest correct version of the selected rate-limiting algorithm.
Focus on correctness first.
Implement:
Per-customer quota
Request accounting
Allow/reject behavior
429 Too Many Requests
Retry-After
Customer isolation
Correct boundary handling
Configuration-driven quotas
Clear code structure
Do NOT yet optimize or add unnecessary production features.
Write focused unit tests for:
Requests below quota
Exactly at quota
One request beyond quota
Independent customers
Window/token reset behavior
Retry behavior
Boundary timestamps
Invalid customer/quota configuration where relevant
Think carefully about off-by-one errors.
Do not merely write tests that confirm your implementation.
First derive the expected behavior independently, then test against it.
At the end provide:
Phase 3 Report
Implementation summary
Important design choices
Tests written
Test results
Edge cases considered
Any discovered bugs
Any remaining concerns
WAIT.
PHASE 4 — Make It Actually Distributed
Now address the most important architectural requirement:
The application must work when requests are distributed across multiple stateless application nodes.
Do NOT fake this by running three copies with independent in-memory counters.
The shared rate-limit state must be coordinated appropriately.
Implement the distributed state mechanism chosen in Phase 1.
Then create a reproducible local multi-node setup.
For example:
Node 1
Node 2
Node 3
↓
Shared rate-limit state
↓
Client/load harness
The exact mechanism should be determined from the architecture phase.
Verify that requests for the same customer hitting different nodes still share the correct quota.
Test:
Same customer → multiple nodes
Different customers → same node
Different customers → different nodes
Concurrent requests
Requests around the quota boundary
Random node distribution
Multiple instances running simultaneously
Be especially suspicious of race conditions.
At the end provide:
Phase 4 Report
How distributed coordination works
Why it is actually distributed
How concurrency is handled
Multi-node test methodology
Test results
Race conditions considered
Any limitations or failure modes
WAIT.
PHASE 5 — Resolve & Encode the Stakeholder Conflict
Now explicitly resolve the CTO vs Support Lead conflict.
Do NOT hide the conflict in implementation details.
We need a defensible engineering decision.
Analyze:
CTO's strict quota requirement
Support's Northwind batch requirement
Whether both can actually be satisfied simultaneously
What requirement takes precedence in our design
What assumption or business decision would be required to satisfy the other side
What we explicitly reject
What configuration mechanism could support a future business exception without hardcoding customer-specific hacks
Avoid:
if customerId == "northwind": ...
unless there is a very strong documented reason and it is clearly NOT being used as an undocumented bypass.
If the correct resolution is that Northwind cannot magically exceed its contracted quota without changing its contract/configuration, state that clearly.
The system should reflect the chosen resolution.
Then update documentation/configuration/tests as necessary.
At the end provide:
Phase 5 Report
Conflict
Options considered
Final decision
Why
What was rejected
How the decision appears in the implementation
How a commercial exception could be represented safely in the future
Tests demonstrating the chosen behavior
WAIT.
PHASE 6 — Build the Load Harness
The load harness is a FIRST-CLASS deliverable.
Do not create a toy script that merely sends requests.
Build a useful, readable harness that can demonstrate:
A customer below quota succeeds.
A customer exactly at quota behaves correctly.
A customer exceeding quota gets rejected.
Two customers have independent budgets.
Requests distributed across three nodes still respect the same customer quota.
Concurrent traffic does not accidentally allow quota leakage.
Boundary behavior is visible.
429 and Retry-After behavior are visible.
The output should be understandable without opening the implementation.
Prefer a clear table or structured report.
For each scenario report useful values such as:
Customer
Configured quota
Requests attempted
Requests accepted
Requests rejected
Status codes
Effective observed rate
Nodes used
Expected result
Actual result
PASS/FAIL
Use deterministic scenarios wherever possible.
Avoid relying solely on timing-sensitive tests.
Where timing is inherently involved, make the assumptions explicit.
At the end run the complete harness.
At the end provide:
Phase 6 Report
Harness architecture
Scenarios
Why each scenario exists
Sample output
What each test proves
What it does NOT prove
Any flaky behavior
Any fixes required
WAIT.
PHASE 7 — Adversarial Testing & Critical Review
Now act as a hostile reviewer.
Assume another engineer will try to reject this submission.
Do NOT immediately modify code.
First inspect the entire implementation and actively look for:
Off-by-one errors
Race conditions
Non-atomic state updates
Per-process state accidentally being used
Incorrect TTL/window behavior
Clock problems
Boundary errors
Customer isolation failures
Incorrect Retry-After
Incorrect status codes
Configuration bugs
Concurrent request leaks
Test weaknesses
Tests that merely test the implementation rather than behavior
False claims in README
Distributed claims that aren't actually demonstrated
Harness weaknesses
Unnecessary complexity
Hidden special cases
Northwind-specific hacks
Poor failure behavior
Unclear assumptions
Missing documentation
Anything that would make an experienced reviewer skeptical
Run the tests and harness.
If you find problems:
Explain the problem first.
Explain why it matters.
Propose the fix.
Implement the fix.
Add a regression test.
Re-run verification.
Do not silently patch problems.
At the end provide:
Phase 7 Report
Issues found
Severity
Root causes
Fixes
Regression tests
Final verification results
Remaining risks
WAIT.
PHASE 8 — Documentation
Now produce reviewer-quality documentation.
Create/update:
solution/README.md
It must explain:
What the service does
Architecture
Algorithm
Why the algorithm was chosen
Distributed coordination
Repository structure
Requirements
Installation
Running the service
Running multiple nodes
Running the harness
Expected output
Configuration
Example requests
Rate-limit behavior
429 behavior
Retry-After
Testing
Known limitations
The reviewer should be able to run the project on a laptop using free tools in approximately 15 minutes.
DECISIONS.md
Keep this concise.
It must explicitly cover:
CTO vs Support conflict
What we decided
What we rejected
Algorithm
Distributed coordination
What the harness proves
What it does not prove
What we would build next with another four hours
Do not turn DECISIONS.md into a huge technical essay.
At the end report:
Documentation completed
Important claims made
Whether every claim is actually supported by tests/evidence
WAIT.
PHASE 9 — Final Submission Audit
Perform a complete submission audit against the ORIGINAL assignment.
Do not trust our previous assumptions.
Re-read the assignment requirements and check each one individually.
Create a checklist:
Requirement
Status
Evidence
Working service
Per-customer limits
Distributed operation
Algorithm documented
Load harness
Boundary demonstrations
README
DECISIONS.md
Session exports
No secrets
Submission structure
For every requirement, provide concrete evidence.
Then inspect the repository for:
Accidental secrets
API keys
Debug files
Temporary files
Build artifacts
Unnecessary dependencies
Broken documentation
Incorrect paths
Missing files
Poor naming
Uncommitted important changes
Tests that don't run from a clean environment
Run the final test suite and final harness.
Do not claim success unless you actually verified it.
At the end provide:
FINAL AUDIT
PASS
Things fully verified.
WARNINGS
Things that work but have limitations.
FAILURES
Anything not completed.
RECOMMENDED FINAL FIXES
Only changes that materially improve the submission.
WAIT.
PHASE 10 — Final Reviewer Simulation
Pretend you are a Trilogy interviewer reviewing this submission.
Read the final repository as if you know nothing about our conversation.
Answer:
Do I understand the candidate's engineering reasoning?
Is the stakeholder conflict clearly resolved?
Is the distributed rate limiter genuinely distributed?
Are quota boundaries actually proven?
Does the harness provide convincing evidence?
Are the tests meaningful?
Are there hidden correctness problems?
Does the candidate understand the tradeoffs?
Is the AI usage transparent?
What would make me reject this candidate?
What would make me strongly recommend this candidate?
What questions would I ask during the interview?
Then, if you identify a serious issue, stop and tell me before making changes.
Otherwise provide the final submission checklist.
WAIT.
CODING/AGENT BEHAVIOR RULES
Throughout the entire process:
1. Inspect before changing
Never modify a file you haven't inspected when its existing content matters.
2. Never assume
If something is unclear, investigate it.
3. Don't bluff
Never say:
"This should work"
"This is distributed"
"The tests pass"
"The race condition is handled"
unless you actually verified it.
4. Show your work
For meaningful changes explain:
What changed
Why
What risk it addresses
How it was tested
5. Prefer small changes
Avoid giant rewrites.
6. Keep the implementation narrow
This assignment explicitly values a narrow, verified, honest solution over unnecessary feature completeness.
7. Treat tests as evidence
A passing test is not automatically proof of correctness.
Ask:
What exactly does this test prove?
8. Challenge your own implementation
After implementing something important, attempt to find a counterexample.
9. No hidden customer hacks
Do not create undocumented Northwind bypasses merely to satisfy the conflicting support requirement.
10. No unnecessary paid infrastructure
Prefer free/local tooling.
11. Preserve the AI transcript
Do not intentionally hide or sanitize important reasoning, failed attempts, debugging, retries, or corrections.
The assignment explicitly evaluates the AI session exports.
12. Do not fabricate work
Never claim that a command was run, test passed, file changed, or behavior was verified unless you actually performed it.
13. Keep me in control
You are the implementation/reasoning agent, but I am the final decision maker.
When an important architectural/business tradeoff appears, explain it and wait for me if the decision is genuinely ambiguous.
RESPONSE FORMAT AFTER EVERY PHASE
Always finish each phase using this structure:
PHASE X COMPLETE
What I did
...
Files changed
...
Key decisions
...
Verification
...
What the evidence proves
...
Remaining concerns
...
Next phase
...
WAITING FOR YOUR INSTRUCTION.
Do NOT start the next phase automatically.
FIRST ACTION
Start with PHASE 0 — Repository & Assignment Reconnaissance.
Do not write implementation code yet.
Inspect the repository and all relevant assignment documents first.
Then give me the Phase 0 report and stop.

# Phase 0 — Repository & Assignment Reconnaissance Report

## 1. What the Assignment Actually Asks

Build a **thin vertical slice** of a per-customer rate-limiting HTTP service for **RelayAPI**, a fictional B2B API platform. The core deliverables are:

### Must Build
1. **Rate-limiting HTTP API/middleware** — enforces per-customer RPM quotas, works across multiple stateless instances (not single-process)
2. **Documented algorithm choice** — one of: token bucket, sliding window, fixed window, leaky bucket, or hybrid — with reasoning tied to RelayAPI's constraints
3. **Load harness** (first-class deliverable) — drives the service at quota boundaries, reports results legibly
4. **Boundary behavior demonstrations** — harness output makes correct/incorrect behavior obvious without reading code

### Must Submit
```
submissions/<github-username>/promise-them-nothing-twice/
├── solution/           # service + harness + README.md (≤15 min setup)
├── sessions/           # AI session exports (.md), chronological
└── DECISIONS.md        # one page, structured prose
```

### Critical: AI Sessions Are the PRIMARY Deliverable
> "This is the primary deliverable we evaluate."

The session exports must show: full prompts, full agent output (tool calls, reasoning, code diffs, errors, retries). Hiding/editing/omitting sessions **disqualifies**.

---

## 2. Stakeholder Conflict

### CTO (Priya Nair) — "Strictly fair, never exceed quota"
- **Hard enforcement**: 429 + `Retry-After` when customer hits RPM limit
- **Per-customer isolation**: Customer A's spike must not affect Customer B
- **Strictly fair metering**: Same tier = same treatment. No hidden bypasses, no manual overrides in production code paths
- **Auditable**: Must explain exactly how requests were counted
- **Distributed**: Must work across 3 stateless nodes
- **Error direction preference**: Would rather over-reject than under-limit (prefers safety)
- **Explicitly rejects**: Single-process rate limiting, "fix in v2", `if (customerId === ...)` hacks

### Support Lead (Marcus Webb) — "Northwind must never see a 429 in batch window"
- **Northwind sees 429 during nightly batch (02:00–04:00 UTC)** — VP of Engineering escalated to CEO
- **Northwind = 60% of revenue**, renewal in 6 weeks
- **Demands**: Northwind must never see 429 during batch window
- **Explicitly rejects**: "Tell them to spread out requests" — their ERP controls schedule
- **Wants**: Temporary exception mechanism, invisible to customer
- **Does NOT ask**: Removing rate limiting for everyone

### The Irreconcilable Truth
From [platform-context.md](file:///Users/miteshvijaybhaichauhan/dev/TrilogyAssignment/briefs/platform-context.md):
- Northwind's contracted tier: **300 RPM**
- Nightly batch actual traffic: **800–1200 RPM** for 90–120 minutes
- This is **2.7x–4x** their contracted quota

**These two requirements are literally contradictory.** The CTO says "never exceed contracted quota." Marcus says "let Northwind exceed their 300 RPM quota by 4x without seeing 429s." Both claim non-negotiable. Neither has authority over the other.

The assignment explicitly says: *"Your job is not to make both memos literally true. Your job is to resolve the conflict explicitly."*

---

## 3. Hard Requirements (Non-negotiable)

| # | Requirement | Source |
|---|------------|--------|
| 1 | Per-customer RPM enforcement | CTO memo |
| 2 | 429 + Retry-After on limit exceeded | CTO memo |
| 3 | Per-customer isolation | CTO memo |
| 4 | Works across 3 stateless nodes | CTO memo, platform context |
| 5 | No single-process-only limiter | CTO memo |
| 6 | Well-understood algorithm | CTO memo |
| 7 | Auditable counting semantics | CTO memo, compliance ask |
| 8 | Customer identity via `X-Customer-Id` header | Platform context |
| 9 | Load harness as first-class deliverable | Assignment |
| 10 | Boundary behavior demonstrated | Assignment |
| 11 | README (≤15 min setup, free tools) | Assignment |
| 12 | DECISIONS.md (one page) | Assignment |
| 13 | AI session exports (full, unedited) | Assignment |
| 14 | No API keys/secrets in submission | Assignment |

## 4. Soft / Negotiable Decisions

| Decision | Options | Notes |
|----------|---------|-------|
| Northwind batch window handling | Raise quota via config, reject with clear docs, hybrid | This IS the conflict to resolve |
| Algorithm choice | Fixed window, sliding window, token bucket, leaky bucket | Must justify |
| Language/framework | Any | Reviewer convenience matters |
| Shared state mechanism | Redis, Postgres, other | Platform context says Redis "may or may not be available" |
| "GA" scope | Thin slice | One endpoint, real limiter, 2+ fake customers, multi-node harness |
| Error direction | Over-reject vs under-limit | CTO prefers over-reject |

---

## 5. Technical Constraints

### Architecture
- **3 stateless app nodes** behind round-robin load balancer
- No sticky sessions
- Nodes do NOT share memory
- TLS terminates at LB → app node → upstream handlers
- Customer identity: `X-Customer-Id` header (trusted)

### Customer Tiers
| Tier | RPM |
|------|-----|
| Starter | 60 |
| Growth | 300 |
| Enterprise | Custom (Northwind: 300) |

### Northwind Specifics
- Contracted 300 RPM
- Actual batch traffic: 800–1200 RPM during 02:00–04:00 UTC
- Their client retries aggressively on 429 (amplification risk)
- Will not re-architect scheduler before renewal

### Data Stores
- Postgres: billing, config
- Redis: cache — **"may or may not be available"** — do not assume ops will provision new infra for a prototype

### Known Pain Points (from wiki)
1. Previous limiter didn't enforce correctly under load-balanced distribution → decommissioned
2. New staging prototype had boundary correctness issues under Northwind-scale traffic → rolled back
3. Compliance: enterprise prospects want one-paragraph explanation of counting semantics

---

## 6. Evaluation Criteria (Directly from Assignment)

| Dimension | What they look for |
|-----------|-------------------|
| **Understanding** | Grasped conflict and constraints BEFORE building |
| **Prompting** | Clear goals, useful context, iterative refinement, recovery from bad agent turns |
| **Critical review** | Catching wrong "distributed" designs, off-by-one windows, tests that prove nothing |
| **Debugging** | Systematic diagnosis when harness and service disagree |
| **Decomposition** | Sequenced work — not one giant prompt |
| **Communication** | Reviewer can follow intent from exports alone |

> "We do not grade variable names, micro-optimizations, or framework fashion."

> "A strong submission is narrow, verified, and honest about tradeoffs — not feature-complete."

---

## 7. Risks / Hidden Traps

### What a naive candidate would do wrong:
1. **Single-process rate limiting** — run 3 instances each with their own in-memory counter (3x actual quota)
2. **Non-atomic distributed updates** — read-then-write race condition allowing quota leakage
3. **Incorrect window boundaries** — off-by-one at quota edge, especially at window resets
4. **Tests that prove nothing** — e.g., send 5 requests against a 100 RPM limit and declare "it works"
5. **Silently hack Northwind** — `if (customerId === "northwind") { bypass }` hidden in code
6. **Ignore the conflict** — implement both literally (impossible) or skip addressing it
7. **Over-engineer** — build a full production system instead of a thin slice
8. **Weak harness** — toy script that fires a few requests, doesn't demonstrate boundary behavior
9. **Fake distribution** — claim "distributed" but only tested on one process
10. **Wrong Retry-After** — returning invalid or unhelpful Retry-After values
11. **Ignore retry amplification** — Northwind's client retries aggressively on 429; a wrong solution makes things worse
12. **Sanitize AI sessions** — hiding mistakes eliminates the primary deliverable

### Technical failure modes:
- Race condition at quota boundary: two nodes each allow the "last" request
- Window reset allowing a burst of 2x quota across boundary
- Clock skew between nodes affecting window calculations
- Redis failure leaving the service in an undefined state
- Non-idempotent request counting

---

## 8. What a Strong Submission Should Demonstrate

1. **Explicitly resolved conflict** — clear reasoning about CTO vs Support, documented in DECISIONS.md
2. **Genuinely distributed** — shared state across nodes, not independent counters
3. **Correct at boundaries** — demonstrated via harness that quota=100, send 100 → all pass, send 101 → 101st rejected
4. **Atomic state updates** — no race conditions at quota edge
5. **Clean architecture** — easy to understand, well-structured
6. **Meaningful tests** — each test proves a specific behavioral claim
7. **Honest limitations** — acknowledge what the solution does NOT guarantee
8. **First-class harness** — structured output, clear scenarios, deterministic where possible
9. **Auditable counting** — simple explanation of how requests are counted
10. **Transparent AI process** — full session exports showing reasoning, mistakes, debugging

---

## 9. Proposed Implementation Phases

| Phase | Description |
|-------|------------|
| **0** | ✅ Repository & Assignment Reconnaissance (this phase) |
| **1** | Architecture & Algorithm Decision — compare algorithms, design distributed coordination, resolve tradeoffs |
| **2** | Technology & Project Skeleton — language/framework selection, project structure, health check, test framework |
| **3** | Core Rate Limiter — single-node correct implementation with unit tests |
| **4** | True Distributed Operation — shared state, multi-node setup, concurrency verification |
| **5** | Stakeholder Conflict Resolution — explicit decision, configuration mechanism, documentation |
| **6** | Load Harness — first-class harness with scenarios, boundary tests, structured output |
| **7** | Adversarial Review — attack own solution, find bugs, regression tests |
| **8** | Documentation — solution/README.md, DECISIONS.md |
| **9** | Final Submission Audit — checklist against original requirements |
| **10** | Reviewer Simulation — final critical review as if we're Trilogy |

---

## 10. Open Questions / Uncertainties Needing Resolution

1. **Redis availability**: Platform context says Redis "may or may not be available." Must decide whether to use Redis (simple, well-understood for rate limiting) or an alternative. Since we control the prototype infrastructure, using Redis seems justified — but this should be an explicit decision.

2. **Conflict resolution direction**: The CTO-vs-Support conflict is the core design decision. My initial assessment:
   - The CTO's position is the **engineering-correct** default: enforce contracted quotas fairly
   - Northwind's problem is a **commercial/contractual** problem, not an engineering one
   - The right engineering answer: provide **configuration-driven quota overrides** so that a business decision to raise Northwind's quota from 300 to 1500 RPM is explicit, audited, and goes through config — not code hacks
   - This satisfies both stakeholders: CTO gets strict enforcement with no hidden bypasses; Support gets a mechanism to resolve the Northwind situation through a commercial quota change
   - **But this is a significant decision — I should present it and wait for your input**

3. **Algorithm choice**: Leaning toward sliding window log or fixed window + counter for simplicity and auditability, but this needs Phase 1 analysis.

4. **"GA" scope**: The platform context defines GA as: "one endpoint, real limiter middleware, config for at least two fake customer IDs including Northwind stand-in, harness that can simulate multi-node deployment." This is explicitly narrow.

5. **Timebox**: 4–6 hours expected. Must be disciplined about scope.

- Redis availability is uncertain, and I'm working within a 4-6 hour timebox to build a thin vertical slice

Now I'm comparing rate limiting algorithms starting with the fixed window counter, weighing how dividing time into fixed calendar-minute buckets per customer would behave under our constraints.

The main flaw I keep coming back to is the boundary burst problem - a customer could send their full quota right at the end of one window and again right at the start of the next, effectively doubling their allowed rate in a short span. But its simplicity, low memory footprint, and clear auditability ("we count requests per calendar minute") make it a strong contender against the CTO's requirements.

Now I'm evaluating the sliding window log approach: storing every request timestamp and counting how many fall within the last 60 seconds eliminates the boundary problem entirely and gives excellent fairness, but at the cost of higher memory (storing up to 300 timestamps per customer for a 300 RPM limit) and needing atomic operations like ZADD, ZRANGEBYSCORE, and ZCARD in a distributed store like Redis.

I'm also comparing the sliding window counter, which blends weighted current and previous fixed-window counts to approximate a rolling limit more cheaply - it uses less memory than the log approach but sacrifices exactness and is harder to explain to customers since it relies on a weighted average rather than a clean rule.

Then I move to the token bucket: quota tokens fill a bucket that drains per request and refills at quota/60 per second, giving controlled bursts based on bucket size, good fairness, and very low memory (just tokens and last refill time), though it needs atomic compare-and-update logic and its auditability is trickier since burst allowance depends on bucket sizing choices.

Leaky bucket, meanwhile, models requests as a queue processed at a fixed output rate, which smooths traffic almost completely with minimal bursting and very fair behavior, but at the cost of complex distributed queue management, higher memory overhead, and added latency that makes it harder to test.

Given the CTO's requirements—strict enforcement, auditability, and a preference for over-rejecting rather than under-limiting—Fixed Window stands out as the easiest to explain to an enterprise customer, even though its calendar-boundary quirk means someone could theoretically send close to double their quota across a boundary if timed precisely.

For 300 RPM that's manageable memory-wise, and with a small number of fake customers for this assignment, memory isn't a real concern anyway. The real challenge is atomicity in Redis — a naive add-then-count sequence isn't atomic across nodes, so I'd need a Lua script to check and increment atomically in one round trip.

Actually, for a simpler fixed-window scheme, I realize I can just use an atomic increment with expiry rather than a sorted set, which simplifies the script considerably.  But I need to guard against a crash between the increment and setting the expiry, since that would leave the key stuck without a TTL, so I should use an atomic script or transaction to set both together.

Actually, the cleanest fix is to encode the time window directly into the key itself, like `rl:{customer_id}:{minute_bucket}`, so the key naturally expires on its own via a TTL set once per new window — that avoids needing complex atomicity beyond a simple INCR-then-conditional-EXPIRE pattern.

I'm leaning toward recommending the Fixed Window Counter approach overall since it's simple to audit and reason about for this use case.

Then I second-guess myself, wondering if a sliding window counter might be worth the small added complexity since it handles boundary bursts better, though it introduces approximation that could clash with the CTO's stricter enforcement preference.

Thinking through harness demonstrability, I compare the three approaches: Fixed Window gives a clean, easy-to-show reset behavior, Sliding Window Log is messier to demonstrate since the window rolls continuously, and Token Bucket depends heavily on timing precision. Fixed Window clearly wins for a clear, demonstrable harness test, so that's what I'll recommend.

Reconsidering the CTO's "never exceed" language, I realize this actually depends on how the quota itself is defined — if it's framed as "requests per calendar minute," then Fixed Window satisfies the contract exactly, and the boundary burst isn't a violation but simply a property of that definition. I'm drafting the compliance language explaining how requests are counted per calendar minute and how the counter resets.

Settling on Fixed Window Counter, I'm now moving to the distributed architecture piece — using Redis as shared state across nodes, with each rate-limit counter keyed by customer and minute timestamp. I'm justifying Redis over alternatives like PostgreSQL, weighing its atomic increments, built-in TTL, and ease of local setup against the platform's caveat that Redis availability isn't guaranteed in production slices.

Writing atomic Lua script...

The script returns whether the request is allowed along with the current count and limit, and this atomicity holds because Redis executes Lua scripts as single uninterruptible operations, ruling out the race condition entirely since INCR itself is atomic and the whole check happens in one unit. For determining the current time window in Fixed Window, I'm weighing whether to trust application node clocks, which risk skew, versus using Redis's own server time for consistency across nodes.

Given the CTO's preference to over-reject rather than under-limit, minor clock skew near a window boundary is tolerable — worst case, a customer sees a slightly shorter effective window. For a single-machine prototype, I'll just use the application node's time to compute the window key and document the clock skew assumption, since Docker containers will share the same clock anyway.

For Retry-After on Fixed Window rejections, I calculate it as 60 minus the current second within the minute, so clients know exactly when the next window opens — with a minimum of 1 second if that value would be zero. Now I'm sketching out the tier configuration structure, mapping starter, growth, and enterprise plans to their requests-per-minute limits.

For customer overrides, the resolution order should check the customer's specific RPM setting first, falling back to their tier default otherwise — so raising Northwind's quota becomes a config change rather than a code change. My recommendation leans toward configuration-driven quotas: the rate limiter is correctly enforcing whatever Northwind's contract specifies, and if the business wants to bump their limit to 1500 RPM, that's an update to their configuration entry rather than a code fix.

This approach satisfies the CTO's demand for strict, auditable, hidden-bypass-free enforcement while still giving Support a real path forward — raise Northwind's configured quota rather than pretending the problem doesn't exist. It explicitly rejects time-based bypasses and customer-specific code branches, while honestly acknowledging that Support's original ask (Northwind never seeing a 429) is really just a request for a higher configured limit, not a technical exemption.

# Phase 1 — Architecture, Algorithm & Distributed Design

---

## Part A — Algorithm Comparison

### 1. Fixed Window Counter

Divide time into **aligned calendar-minute buckets** (e.g., `10:00:00–10:00:59`, `10:01:00–10:01:59`). Maintain one counter per customer per window. Increment on each request; reject when counter exceeds quota.

| Criterion | Analysis for RelayAPI |
|-----------|----------------------|
| **Strict RPM enforcement** | ✅ Strictly enforces within each defined window. A customer with 100 RPM will never get >100 in any single calendar minute. |
| **Boundary correctness** | ⚠️ Classic boundary burst: 100 requests at `10:00:58` + 100 at `10:01:01` = 200 in ~3 seconds. Not a violation if "RPM" is defined as "per calendar minute," but looks alarming. |
| **Burst behavior** | Allows full quota in first second of window. Entire budget consumed instantly → idle rest of minute. |
| **Fairness** | ✅ Same tier = same counter logic. No customer-specific paths. |
| **Concurrent requests** | ✅ Single atomic `INCR` — no read-modify-write race. |
| **Distributed implementation** | ✅ One key per customer per window in shared store. All nodes hit same key. |
| **Atomicity requirements** | Very low. Redis `INCR` is natively atomic. Lua script bundles INCR + EXPIRE + check. |
| **Memory usage** | Minimal: 1 key per customer per active window. |
| **Implementation complexity** | **Lowest** of all candidates. |
| **Auditability** | **Best.** One paragraph: "We count requests in each calendar minute. At the limit, further requests get 429 until the next minute." |
| **Retry-After calculation** | Trivial: `60 - (unix_seconds % 60)`. Deterministic. |
| **Load-harness demonstrability** | **Best.** Send exactly N requests → all pass. Send N+1 → rejected. Wait for window → budget resets. Clear, deterministic. |
| **Suitability for this assignment** | **High.** Matches CTO's auditability requirement. Simple to implement correctly. Easy to demonstrate. Boundary burst is a documented limitation, not a correctness bug. |

### 2. Sliding Window Log

Store the **timestamp of every request** in a sorted set. For each new request, count entries within the last 60 seconds.

| Criterion | Analysis for RelayAPI |
|-----------|----------------------|
| **Strict RPM enforcement** | ✅ Strictest possible. No more than N requests in ANY rolling 60-second window. |
| **Boundary correctness** | ✅ No boundary burst problem. |
| **Burst behavior** | Allows burst within 60s, but burst at boundary is impossible. |
| **Fairness** | ✅ Identical treatment for same tier. |
| **Concurrent requests** | ⚠️ Requires atomic add-and-count. Sorted set operations must be bundled. |
| **Distributed implementation** | ✅ Sorted set per customer in shared store. |
| **Atomicity requirements** | **Medium.** Needs Lua script: ZREMRANGEBYSCORE + ZCARD + ZADD in one atomic block. |
| **Memory usage** | **O(quota) per customer.** For 300 RPM: 300 entries. Acceptable for prototype, poor at scale. |
| **Implementation complexity** | Medium. Sorted set operations, unique member generation, cleanup logic. |
| **Auditability** | Good but harder: "We track every request timestamp and count how many fall within the last 60 seconds." |
| **Retry-After calculation** | **Complex.** Must find the oldest entry in the window and compute when it expires: `oldest_timestamp + 60 - now`. |
| **Load-harness demonstrability** | **Harder.** Rolling window means timing of each request matters. Tests become timing-sensitive. |
| **Suitability for this assignment** | Medium. Strictest semantics but harder to demonstrate, harder to explain to compliance, and more complex for a 4–6 hour budget. |

### 3. Sliding Window Counter (Hybrid)

Approximate a sliding window by **weighting** the previous fixed-window count with the current one based on elapsed time in the current window.

| Criterion | Analysis for RelayAPI |
|-----------|----------------------|
| **Strict RPM enforcement** | ⚠️ **Approximate.** The count is an estimate. Can allow slightly above or below quota. |
| **Boundary correctness** | Better than fixed window, but not exact. |
| **Burst behavior** | Smoother than fixed window. |
| **Fairness** | ⚠️ Approximate fairness — two customers on the same tier may get slightly different effective limits depending on traffic shape. |
| **Concurrent requests** | ⚠️ Requires reading two counters and computing a weight — more complex atomicity. |
| **Distributed implementation** | Two keys per customer (current + previous window). |
| **Atomicity requirements** | **High.** Read two keys + compute weight + decide + increment must be atomic. |
| **Memory usage** | Low: 2 keys per customer. |
| **Implementation complexity** | Medium. |
| **Auditability** | **Poor.** "We use a weighted average of two adjacent windows." Enterprise compliance will ask: "So what is my EXACT limit?" Answer: "It depends on the position within the window." This is exactly the "it's complicated" the CTO rejected. |
| **Retry-After calculation** | **Approximate.** Cannot give a precise retry time because the weight changes continuously. |
| **Load-harness demonstrability** | **Poor.** Hard to demonstrate exact boundaries because the effective limit shifts within each window. |
| **Suitability for this assignment** | **Low.** The approximation directly conflicts with the CTO's "not 'mostly,' not 'on average' — never" requirement and the auditability demand. |

### 4. Token Bucket

Each customer has a bucket of `N` tokens (= quota). Tokens refill at `quota/60` per second. Each request consumes one token. Reject when bucket is empty.

| Criterion | Analysis for RelayAPI |
|-----------|----------------------|
| **Strict RPM enforcement** | ⚠️ Depends on bucket size. If bucket size = quota, a customer can consume all tokens instantly and then must wait a full minute. Over 60s they get exactly their quota. But the burst is front-loaded. |
| **Boundary correctness** | ✅ No fixed window boundary problem. Smooth refill. |
| **Burst behavior** | Allows burst up to bucket size. Can be tuned. |
| **Fairness** | ✅ Same bucket config = same treatment. |
| **Concurrent requests** | ⚠️ Requires atomic read-compute-update: read tokens + last_refill → compute current tokens → decrement → write. |
| **Distributed implementation** | Store `{tokens_remaining, last_refill_timestamp}` in shared store. |
| **Atomicity requirements** | **Medium-High.** The refill calculation + decrement + write must be atomic. Requires Lua script. |
| **Memory usage** | Very low: 2 values per customer. |
| **Implementation complexity** | Medium. Refill calculation requires floating-point time math. |
| **Auditability** | Medium. "Your bucket starts with N tokens. Tokens refill at N/60 per second. Each request uses one token." Understandable but not as intuitive as "N per minute." |
| **Retry-After calculation** | Clean: `1 / refill_rate` = time until 1 token is available. |
| **Load-harness demonstrability** | **Timing-sensitive.** Refill is continuous. Hard to create deterministic boundary tests. |
| **Suitability for this assignment** | Medium. Well-understood algorithm. But the continuous refill makes it harder to demonstrate precise boundaries in the harness, and the auditability story is slightly weaker than Fixed Window. |

### 5. Leaky Bucket

Requests enter a queue. Queue drains at a fixed rate. If queue is full, reject. Effectively smooths all traffic to a constant rate.

| Criterion | Analysis for RelayAPI |
|-----------|----------------------|
| **Strict RPM enforcement** | ✅ Strict: exactly `quota/60` requests per second exit the queue. |
| **Boundary correctness** | ✅ No boundary problem — no windows. |
| **Burst behavior** | **Minimal.** Smooths everything. This is a disadvantage — legitimate bursts within quota are delayed. |
| **Fairness** | ✅ Very fair — identical smoothing for same tier. |
| **Concurrent requests** | ⚠️ Requires distributed queue management. |
| **Distributed implementation** | **Hard.** Distributed queue with fixed drain rate across nodes is significantly complex. |
| **Atomicity requirements** | **High.** Queue operations must be globally consistent. |
| **Memory usage** | Queue storage: O(queue depth) per customer. |
| **Implementation complexity** | **Highest.** Distributed FIFO queue with fixed drain rate. |
| **Auditability** | Medium. "Requests are processed at a fixed rate." But: introduces latency. |
| **Retry-After calculation** | Queue depth / drain rate. |
| **Load-harness demonstrability** | **Poor.** Introduces latency; tests must account for queueing delays. |
| **Suitability for this assignment** | **Low.** Over-engineered for this assignment. The queuing semantics are inappropriate — RelayAPI is a pass-through API, not a job queue. Introducing request latency is a different product decision. |

---

## Part B — Adversarial Counterexamples

### Fixed Window — Boundary Burst Attack

```
Quota: 100 RPM

Timeline:
  10:00:50.000  →  Send 100 requests  →  All accepted (window 10:00)
  10:01:00.001  →  Send 100 requests  →  All accepted (window 10:01)

Result: 200 requests in ~10 seconds
```

**Is this a violation?** It depends entirely on how we define "RPM":
- If RPM = "per calendar minute" → **Not a violation.** Each minute got exactly 100. The contract is satisfied.
- If RPM = "in any rolling 60-second window" → **Violation.** 200 requests in a 10-second span clearly exceeds 100/60s.

**My assessment:** This is a **known, documented limitation**, not a correctness bug. The CTO's auditability requirement ("explain to an enterprise prospect *exactly* how we counted") is best served by a clean definition. "We count per calendar minute" is cleaner than "we track rolling windows."

The CTO's own success criterion: *"Show me a demo where two customers on a 100 RPM tier each get exactly their budget."* The word "exactly" aligns with a fixed-window counter more than a rolling approximation.

**Mitigation:** Document the boundary behavior honestly. If it's unacceptable, the algorithm can be upgraded to Sliding Window Log — but that's a complexity/auditability tradeoff for future consideration.

### Sliding Window Log — Stale Entry Attack

```
Quota: 100 RPM

Timeline:
  10:00:00.000  →  Send 100 requests  →  All accepted
  10:00:30.000  →  Send 1 request     →  Rejected (100 entries in last 60s)
  10:01:00.001  →  Send 1 request     →  Accepted (first batch expires)

What if cleanup race? Two nodes simultaneously try ZREMRANGEBYSCORE:
  Node 1: ZREMRANGEBYSCORE key -inf (now-60)  →  removes 100 entries
  Node 2: ZREMRANGEBYSCORE key -inf (now-60)  →  removes 0 entries (already gone)
  Both: ZADD their new request
  Both: ZCARD → 2
  Both: 2 < 100 → allow
```

**Assessment:** This isn't actually a problem IF cleanup + add + count are in a single Lua script. But if implemented as separate Redis commands, there IS a race. The Lua script approach handles this correctly.

**True failure mode:** The sorted set grows to `quota` entries per customer. For Northwind at 300 RPM with aggressive retries (800+ RPM), the sorted set churns heavily. Each rejected request still needs cleanup + count. Under load, this means ~1200 Redis operations per minute per customer, each executing a Lua script with sorted set operations. This is heavier than Fixed Window's simple INCR.

### Token Bucket — Refill Timing Attack

```
Quota: 100 RPM  →  Refill rate: 100/60 ≈ 1.667 tokens/sec

Timeline:
  10:00:00.000  →  Bucket has 100 tokens.  Send 100 → all accepted. Bucket: 0.
  10:00:00.600  →  Refill: 0.6 * 1.667 = 1.0 token.  Send 1 → accepted.
  10:00:01.200  →  Refill: 0.6 * 1.667 = 1.0 token.  Send 1 → accepted.
  ...
  10:01:00.000  →  Total requests sent: 100 + 100 = 200 in 60 seconds.
```

Wait — this can't happen. After consuming 100, the bucket is at 0. Refill at 1.667/sec for 60 seconds = 100 tokens. So total in 60s = 100 + 100 = 200? No.

Actually: The 100 requests are consumed at t=0. Then over the next 60 seconds, 100 tokens refill. But the customer already used 100 at t=0. So in the FIRST 60 seconds, they can consume up to 100 (burst) + (time_remaining * refill_rate) tokens.

At t=0: consume 100. At t=60: 100 tokens refilled. Total in first 60s: 100 + 100 = 200? No, because the bucket caps at 100. The refilled tokens don't exceed the bucket size. But if the customer consumes them as they refill...

t=0: bucket=100, consume 100, bucket=0
t=0.6: bucket≈1, consume 1, bucket=0
t=1.2: bucket≈1, consume 1, bucket=0
...
In 60 seconds after the burst: 100 * (1.667 * 0.6) ... actually 60 * 1.667 = 100 more tokens refilled and consumed.

So total in 120 seconds: 100 (burst) + 100 (refilled in first 60s) + 100 (refilled in second 60s) = 300 in 120s = 150/min average.

But in the FIRST 60 seconds: 100 (burst at t=0) + ~100 (refilled and consumed) = ~200. That's 2x the quota in the first minute!

**This is a real problem with Token Bucket.** If bucket size = quota, the first minute can see up to 2x quota. You can fix this by setting bucket size = quota and making refill only start when the bucket isn't full... but that changes the semantics.

The standard fix is: set bucket size much smaller than quota. But then the bucket doesn't represent "RPM" in any intuitive way.

**Assessment:** Token Bucket's relationship between bucket size, refill rate, and "RPM" is not intuitive for auditability. The CTO wants to say "100 RPM" and mean exactly that.

### Sliding Window Counter — Approximation Error

```
Quota: 100 RPM
Previous window count: 80
Current window count: 30
Position in current window: 0.5 (halfway through)

Weighted count: 80 * (1 - 0.5) + 30 = 40 + 30 = 70
→ Allow (70 < 100)

But actual requests in last 60 seconds might be very different depending on
WHEN in the previous window those 80 requests arrived.
If all 80 arrived in the last 10 seconds of the previous window, then actual
rolling count ≈ 80 + 30 = 110 > 100.

The approximation UNDER-counts in this case → allows requests past quota.
```

**Assessment:** This directly violates the CTO's "never exceed" requirement. The approximation can go in either direction: under-count (violating the CTO) or over-count (rejecting legitimate requests). The CTO prefers over-reject, but an algorithm that is inherently approximate is difficult to defend when the requirement says "never."

---

## Part C — What "100 RPM" Actually Means

### Definition

> **"100 RPM" means: at most 100 requests from this customer are permitted within each aligned calendar minute (UTC).**

A "calendar minute" runs from `HH:MM:00.000` to `HH:MM:59.999`.

### Precise Behavior

| Time | Event | Counter | Decision |
|------|-------|---------|----------|
| `10:00:00.000` | Window `10:00` begins | 0 | — |
| `10:00:00.001` | Request 1 | 1 | ✅ Allow |
| `10:00:45.000` | Request 99 | 99 | ✅ Allow |
| `10:00:45.001` | Request 100 | 100 | ✅ Allow (exactly at quota) |
| `10:00:45.002` | Request 101 | 100 (not incremented) | ❌ 429 |
| `10:00:59.999` | Request 150 | 100 | ❌ 429 |
| `10:01:00.000` | Window `10:01` begins | 0 | — |
| `10:01:00.001` | Request 1 (new window) | 1 | ✅ Allow |

### Concurrent Requests at Boundary

Two requests arrive simultaneously at count=99:
- Node 1: `INCR` → gets 100 → ✅ Allow
- Node 2: `INCR` → gets 101 → ❌ Reject

Redis `INCR` is atomic and sequential. Exactly one request gets count=100 (allowed), the next gets 101 (rejected). No ambiguity.

### Compliance Paragraph

> *"RelayAPI counts each customer's requests within aligned calendar minutes (UTC). A minute runs from :00 to :59 seconds. When the count for a given minute reaches the customer's contracted limit, all further requests in that minute receive HTTP 429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After header indicating when the next minute begins. The counter resets to zero at the start of each new minute. Counting is performed in a shared data store that all application nodes access, ensuring the limit is global — not per-node."*

---

## Part D — Distributed Architecture

```
                    ┌──────────────────┐
                    │   Load Balancer   │
                    │  (round-robin)    │
                    └────────┬─────────┘
                             │
              ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
              ↓              ↓              ↓
        ┌──────────┐   ┌──────────┐   ┌──────────┐
        │  Node 1  │   │  Node 2  │   │  Node 3  │
        │ :3001    │   │ :3002    │   │ :3003    │
        │          │   │          │   │          │
        │ Stateless│   │ Stateless│   │ Stateless│
        │ App      │   │ App      │   │ App      │
        └────┬─────┘   └────┬─────┘   └────┬─────┘
             │              │              │
             └──────────────┼──────────────┘
                            ↓
                   ┌─────────────────┐
                   │     Redis       │
                   │  (shared state) │
                   │  :6379          │
                   └─────────────────┘
```

### Why nodes remain stateless
Each node has **zero rate-limit state** in its own memory. All quota accounting happens in Redis. Any node can serve any customer's request. If a node restarts, nothing is lost. Load balancer can distribute freely.

### How different nodes see the same customer budget
All nodes execute the same Lua script against the same Redis key: `rl:{customer_id}:{minute_window}`. Redis is single-threaded — scripts execute atomically and sequentially. Whether request 99 comes from Node 1 and request 100 from Node 3, they both atomically increment the same counter.

### Multiple nodes attempt the same customer's final available request
```
Counter = 99, Quota = 100

Node 1: INCR → 100 → ≤ 100 → Allow
Node 2: INCR → 101 → > 100 → Reject

This happens atomically inside Redis. No race possible.
```

### Shared state unavailable (Redis down)
**Decision: Fail closed (reject all requests with 503 Service Unavailable).**

Why:
- CTO explicitly prefers "under-limiting, not over-limiting" — but actually says "I would rather reject a few extra legitimate requests than let someone blow past quota."
- Fail-open during Redis outage means unlimited requests — directly violates the CTO's core requirement.
- Fail-closed is conservative and consistent with the CTO's stated preference.
- In practice, if Redis is down, the service has bigger problems. A 503 is honest.

---

## Part E — Shared State Technology Comparison

### Option 1: Redis

| Factor | Assessment |
|--------|------------|
| **Atomic operations** | ✅ `INCR` is natively atomic. Lua scripts execute atomically. |
| **Concurrency** | ✅ Single-threaded execution model. No concurrent access races. |
| **TTL/expiry** | ✅ Native `EXPIRE` command. Keys auto-cleanup. |
| **Distributed correctness** | ✅ All nodes talk to same instance. Single source of truth. |
| **Local setup** | ✅ `docker run redis` or `brew install redis`. < 1 minute. |
| **Complexity** | Low. Well-understood patterns for rate limiting. |
| **Auditability** | ✅ Can inspect current counters with `GET`. |
| **Failure behavior** | Connection failure → fail closed (503). Clear. |
| **Assignment fit** | ✅ Free, laptop-friendly, well-understood, minimal setup. |

### Option 2: PostgreSQL

| Factor | Assessment |
|--------|------------|
| **Atomic operations** | ⚠️ Requires `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE` with row-level locking, or advisory locks. |
| **Concurrency** | ⚠️ Row-level locks work but are heavier. MVCC adds complexity. |
| **TTL/expiry** | ❌ No native TTL. Requires background cleanup or WHERE clauses. |
| **Distributed correctness** | ✅ Same database = same state. |
| **Local setup** | ⚠️ Heavier than Redis. Needs schema creation. |
| **Complexity** | Medium-High. SQL, transactions, migrations, connection pooling. |
| **Auditability** | ✅ SQL queries on counter table. |
| **Failure behavior** | Transaction rollback. |
| **Assignment fit** | ⚠️ Overkill for a counter. The platform context mentions Postgres for "billing, config" — using it for high-frequency counters is a mismatch. |

### Option 3: In-Process Memory

| Factor | Assessment |
|--------|------------|
| **Distributed correctness** | ❌ **FAILS THE CORE REQUIREMENT.** Three nodes = three independent counters = 3x quota. |

**Eliminated.** This is explicitly called out in the CTO memo as unacceptable: *"A rate limiter that only works in a single process and gets deployed three times."*

### Option 4: SQLite (Shared File)

| Factor | Assessment |
|--------|------------|
| **Distributed correctness** | ❌ SQLite is designed for single-process access. Multiple processes accessing the same file leads to locking issues. Not designed for concurrent network access. |

**Eliminated.**

### Decision: Redis

**Justification for using Redis despite "may or may not be available":**

The platform context says Redis is cache infrastructure that *"may or may not be available in your slice; do not assume ops will provision new infra for a prototype."*

This refers to the **production ops team** provisioning infrastructure. For our **GA prototype**, we control the development environment. We provision Redis ourselves — it's a `docker run` command. The platform context is warning against assuming existing production Redis infrastructure, not forbidding us from including Redis in our solution.

Additionally:
- Redis is free and open source
- Runs on any developer laptop
- Standard tool for rate limiting
- Docker-friendy (single container)
- No licensing, no accounts, no cloud dependency
- A reviewer can start it in seconds

If Redis were truly forbidden, the assignment would say so explicitly. The "may or may not" language tests whether candidates think about infrastructure assumptions — not whether they avoid Redis entirely.

---

## Part F — Atomicity Design

### The Race Condition

```
WITHOUT atomicity:

  Node 1: READ counter → 99
  Node 2: READ counter → 99
  Node 1: 99 < 100 → ALLOW → WRITE 100
  Node 2: 99 < 100 → ALLOW → WRITE 100

  Result: TWO requests allowed at the boundary.
  Customer effectively got 101 requests.
  VIOLATION of quota.
```

This is incorrect because the read-decide-write sequence is not atomic. Between Node 1's read and Node 2's read, no state change is visible.

### The Solution: Redis Lua Script

```lua
-- rate_limit.lua
-- Executes atomically in Redis (single-threaded, no interruption)

local key     = KEYS[1]            -- "rl:{customer_id}:{window}"
local limit   = tonumber(ARGV[1])  -- e.g., 100
local ttl     = tonumber(ARGV[2])  -- e.g., 60 (seconds)

-- Atomic increment
local current = redis.call('INCR', key)

-- Set expiry only on first request in this window
if current == 1 then
    redis.call('EXPIRE', key, ttl)
end

if current <= limit then
    -- ALLOWED
    return { 1, current, limit }       -- {allowed, count, limit}
else
    -- REJECTED — do NOT count this request against future quota
    -- (counter already incremented, but that's fine —
    --  it only means subsequent requests also get rejected,
    --  which is the correct behavior)
    return { 0, current, limit }       -- {rejected, count, limit}
end
```

**Why this is atomic:**
1. Redis executes Lua scripts as a **single atomic unit**. No other Redis command can interleave.
2. `INCR` itself is atomic — it reads, increments, and returns the new value in one operation.
3. The script combines INCR + EXPIRE + comparison into one indivisible operation.
4. Two nodes calling this script simultaneously will serialize: one gets `100`, the next gets `101`.

**Edge case — EXPIRE not set:** If `INCR` succeeds but the script crashes before `EXPIRE`, the key persists forever. However: (a) Lua scripts in Redis execute atomically — partial execution doesn't happen; (b) we set EXPIRE only when `current == 1` (first request), and the script is atomic, so this race doesn't exist.

**Edge case — Counter exceeds limit:** When a rejected request still increments the counter (e.g., counter goes to 150 even though quota is 100), this is harmless. Every value > 100 maps to "reject." The counter simply reflects total attempts, which is actually useful for auditing.

### Alternative considered: INCR without Lua

```
INCR key → get count
If count == 1: EXPIRE key 60
If count > limit: reject
```

This has a micro-race: if the process crashes between `INCR` (first request) and `EXPIRE`, the key never expires. Lua script eliminates this. For a prototype this risk is extremely low, but the Lua script costs us nothing and is definitively correct.

---

## Part G — Clock / Time Semantics

### Time Source

**Decision: Use the application node's system clock (UTC) to determine the current window.**

The window key is computed as:
```
window_id = floor(unix_timestamp_seconds / 60)
```

For example, at `2026-03-14 10:05:37 UTC`:
```
unix_timestamp = 1773588337
window_id = 1773588337 / 60 = 29559805
key = "rl:northwind:29559805"
```

### Clock Skew Analysis

**In our prototype**: All nodes run on the same machine (Docker containers or local processes). Clock skew is **zero** — they all use the host's clock.

**In production (if deployed)**: Nodes on different machines could have clock skew of up to a few seconds (with NTP). Worst case:
- Node 1 thinks it's `10:00:59` (window A)
- Node 2 thinks it's `10:01:01` (window B)
- Same customer, same second — requests counted in different windows

Impact: During a ~1-second transition period, some requests go to the old window and some to the new one. This means the customer might get slightly MORE than their quota across the boundary (some counted in old window, some in new).

**Mitigation for production:** Use Redis `TIME` command to get canonical time. But this adds a round-trip per request.

**For this assignment:** Document the assumption. On a single machine, clock skew is not a factor. In production, Redis `TIME` would be the fix.

### Retry-After Calculation

Based on application node clock:
```
retry_after_seconds = 60 - (unix_timestamp_seconds % 60)
```

If `retry_after_seconds == 0`, return `1` (minimum useful value).

---

## Part H — Retry-After Semantics

### Response Format

```http
HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
Content-Type: application/json
Retry-After: 23
X-RateLimit-Limit: 100
X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0
X-RateLimit-Reset: 1773588360

{
  "error": "rate_limit_exceeded",
  "message": "Rate limit exceeded. Try again in 23 seconds.",
  "retry_after": 23,
  "limit": 100,
  "window_reset": 1773588360
}
```

### Calculation

```
current_time = unix_timestamp_seconds (e.g., 1773588337)
window_end = (floor(current_time / 60) + 1) * 60  (e.g., 1773588360)
retry_after = window_end - current_time  (e.g., 23)
retry_after = max(retry_after, 1)  -- minimum 1 second
```

### Edge Cases

| Scenario | Retry-After | Notes |
|----------|-------------|-------|
| Rejected at :00 | 60 | Full minute to wait |
| Rejected at :30 | 30 | Half minute |
| Rejected at :59 | 1 | Minimum 1 second |
| Rejected at :59.9 | 1 | Rounds up to 1 |

### Successful Response Headers

Even on successful requests, we include rate-limit headers so clients can self-regulate:

```http
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
X-RateLimit-Limit: 100
X-RateLimit-Remaining: 37
X-RateLimit-Reset: 1773588360
```

---

## Part I — Customer Configuration Model

### Design

```yaml
# config.yaml (or equivalent in-code configuration)

tiers:
  starter:
    rpm: 60
  growth:
    rpm: 300
  enterprise:
    rpm: 300        # default for enterprise tier

customers:
  customer-1:
    name: "Acme Corp"
    tier: starter
    # no rpm override → uses tier default (60)

  customer-2:
    name: "Beta Inc"
    tier: growth
    # no rpm override → uses tier default (300)

  northwind:
    name: "Northwind Logistics"
    tier: enterprise
    # no rpm override → uses tier default (300)
    # To accommodate batch window: change this to rpm: 1500
    # That is a COMMERCIAL decision, not an engineering one
```

### Resolution Logic

```
resolve_quota(customer_id):
  customer = customers[customer_id]
  if customer has explicit rpm override:
    return customer.rpm
  else:
    return tiers[customer.tier].rpm
```

### How a Business Quota Change Works

If the business decides Northwind should get 1500 RPM:

1. **Commercial decision** is made (sales/leadership approve)
2. Configuration is updated: `northwind.rpm: 1500`
3. Service restarts or reloads config
4. Rate limiter enforces the NEW quota — no code change needed
5. **Audit trail**: config change is version-controlled

This is exactly what the CTO asked for: *"If we ever grant a commercial exception, it goes through config and audit — not a midnight commit."*

### Unknown Customer Handling

If `X-Customer-Id` is not in the configuration:
- **Option A**: Reject with 401 (unknown customer)
- **Option B**: Apply a restrictive default (e.g., Starter tier)

**Decision**: Reject with 401. An unknown customer shouldn't be reaching the API at all — the platform context says the header is "trusted from API gateway today." An unknown customer ID indicates a configuration problem, not normal traffic.

---

## Part J — CTO vs Support Conflict Resolution

### The Conflict (restated precisely)

- **CTO**: "A customer must never exceed their contracted quota. No hidden bypasses."
- **Support**: "Northwind must never see a 429 during their batch window."
- **Fact**: Northwind's contracted quota is 300 RPM. Their batch sends 800–1200 RPM.
- **Arithmetic**: 800 ≤ x ≤ 1200 > 300. These requirements are **mutually exclusive** with the current contract.

### Options Evaluated

#### Option A: Strictly enforce 300 RPM, reject Northwind during batch

| Aspect | Assessment |
|--------|------------|
| CTO satisfied? | ✅ Yes — strict enforcement, fair, auditable |
| Support satisfied? | ❌ No — Northwind sees 429s, VP escalates |
| Engineering | Correct. The limiter does what it's configured to do. |
| Fairness | ✅ All customers treated identically by the system |
| Auditability | ✅ Nothing hidden |
| Risk | Business risk: Northwind may leave (60% revenue) |

#### Option B: Configuration-driven quota increase for Northwind

| Aspect | Assessment |
|--------|------------|
| CTO satisfied? | ✅ Yes — enforcement is strict, change goes through config, auditable, no code hacks |
| Support satisfied? | ✅ Yes — if Northwind's quota is raised to 1500 RPM, they won't see 429s |
| Engineering | The limiter doesn't know about "batch windows." It enforces whatever quota is configured. A commercial decision to raise the quota is a business input to the system. |
| Fairness | ✅ Same mechanism for all customers. If any customer negotiates a higher quota, it's configured the same way. |
| Auditability | ✅ Config change is versioned. Quota is explicit. |
| Risk | Requires a business decision to change the contract. Engineering provides the mechanism; business provides the decision. |

#### Option C: Time-based bypass (batch window exception)

| Aspect | Assessment |
|--------|------------|
| CTO satisfied? | ❌ No — this IS a hidden bypass. "During 02:00-04:00 UTC, Northwind gets a different limit" is exactly the kind of special-case hack the CTO rejected. |
| Support satisfied? | ✅ Yes |
| Engineering | Adds complexity: time-of-day logic, customer-specific windows, timezone handling. |
| Fairness | ❌ Violates fairness. Same tier, different treatment. |
| Auditability | ⚠️ "Your quota is 300 RPM, except between 2-4 AM when it's... different." Hard to explain to compliance. |
| Risk | Sets precedent for customer-specific time-based exceptions. Maintenance burden. |

#### Option D: Separate "burst" product tier

| Aspect | Assessment |
|--------|------------|
| Engineering | Over-engineered for a 4–6 hour prototype. Introduces tier management, burst quotas, burst windows. |
| Assignment fit | Exceeds thin vertical slice. |

### ✅ RECOMMENDED: Option B — Configuration-Driven Quota

**The engineering system does not "know" about Northwind's batch window.** The system enforces the configured quota, period. If the business decides to raise Northwind's quota from 300 to 1500 RPM:

1. That is a **commercial/contractual decision** made by business leadership
2. It is reflected as a **configuration change**: `northwind.rpm: 1500`
3. The rate limiter enforces the new limit **using the same code path as every other customer**
4. It is **auditable**: the config change is in version control
5. It is **fair**: any customer can get their quota adjusted through the same mechanism
6. There is **no hidden bypass**: the quota is explicit

**What we explicitly reject:**
- Time-based exception windows
- `if (customerId === "northwind")` code paths
- Invisible overrides or "soft" limits
- Any mechanism that cannot be explained to a compliance auditor

**What we acknowledge:**
- With Northwind's current contracted 300 RPM, they **will** see 429s during their batch
- Resolving this requires a business decision to change their contracted quota
- Engineering provides the mechanism (configurable per-customer RPM); business provides the input
- This is the honest engineering answer

**In our prototype:**
- We ship Northwind with 300 RPM (their current contract)
- We document that raising it to 1500 is a one-line config change
- We demonstrate that the system correctly enforces whatever is configured
- DECISIONS.md explains the conflict, our choice, and why

---

## Part K — Failure Mode Analysis

| # | Failure Mode | Expected Behavior | Why | Test? |
|---|-------------|-------------------|-----|-------|
| 1 | **Redis unavailable** | Return 503 to all requests | Fail-closed: CTO prefers over-reject. Without shared state, cannot guarantee quota. | ✅ Manual test |
| 2 | **Node crashes mid-request** | Request is lost; counter may or may not have incremented | Atomic Lua script: either fully executes or doesn't. No partial state. | No (infrastructure level) |
| 3 | **Two nodes, same customer, concurrent requests at boundary** | Exactly one gets the last slot, other gets 429 | Redis INCR atomicity in Lua script | ✅ Harness Scenario 6 |
| 4 | **Customer sends exactly quota requests** | All accepted, count = quota | Counter ≤ limit → allow | ✅ Harness Scenario 2 |
| 5 | **Customer sends quota + 1** | First quota accepted, last one rejected with 429 | Counter > limit → reject | ✅ Harness Scenario 3 |
| 6 | **Traffic crosses window boundary** | Old window's requests don't affect new window | Separate Redis keys per window; old key expires | ✅ Harness Scenario 7 |
| 7 | **Multiple customers simultaneously** | Independent counters, no interference | Separate Redis keys per customer | ✅ Harness Scenario 4 |
| 8 | **Clock skew between nodes** | At window boundary, some requests may land in different windows | On single machine: no skew. In production: documented limitation. | No (same-machine prototype) |
| 9 | **Redis latency** | Requests wait for Redis response; latency added to response time | Synchronous call. No timeout = hung request. We should set a connection timeout. | ⚠️ Document |
| 10 | **Redis race condition** | Cannot occur — Lua scripts are atomic | Redis is single-threaded; Lua scripts execute without interruption | ✅ Harness Scenario 6 |
| 11 | **Northwind sends 1200 RPM at 300 RPM config** | 300 accepted, 900 rejected per minute | System correctly enforces configured quota | ✅ Harness Scenario 3 (scaled) |
| 12 | **Client retries 429 aggressively** | Each retry counts as a new request (still exceeds quota, still rejected) | Counter increments on every attempt (including rejected ones, which only pushes counter further past limit) | Document |
| 13 | **Uneven LB distribution** | Doesn't matter — shared state. Whether 100 requests go to 1 node or split across 3, same Redis key | All nodes talk to same Redis | ✅ Harness Scenario 5 |
| 14 | **Application restarts** | No state lost — all state is in Redis. New process reconnects. | Stateless nodes by design | No (infrastructure) |

---

## Part L — Load Harness Design

### Harness Architecture

The harness is a standalone program that:
1. Starts with a clean Redis state (flush relevant keys)
2. Sends HTTP requests to the service (via load balancer or directly to nodes)
3. Counts responses by status code
4. Prints a structured report

### Scenarios

#### Scenario 1: Below Quota
| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| **Input** | Customer A (100 RPM), send 50 requests |
| **Expected** | 50 accepted (200), 0 rejected |
| **Pass/Fail** | accepted == 50, rejected == 0 |
| **Proves** | Requests under quota are allowed |

#### Scenario 2: Exactly at Quota
| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| **Input** | Customer A (100 RPM), send exactly 100 requests |
| **Expected** | 100 accepted (200), 0 rejected |
| **Pass/Fail** | accepted == 100, rejected == 0 |
| **Proves** | Customer gets their full budget |

#### Scenario 3: Quota + 1 (One Over)
| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| **Input** | Customer A (100 RPM), send 105 requests |
| **Expected** | 100 accepted, 5 rejected (429) |
| **Pass/Fail** | accepted == 100, rejected == 5 |
| **Proves** | Requests beyond quota are rejected. Boundary is exactly at quota, not off-by-one. |

#### Scenario 4: Customer Isolation
| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| **Input** | Customer A (100 RPM) sends 100; Customer B (60 RPM) sends 60 |
| **Expected** | A: 100 accepted, 0 rejected. B: 60 accepted, 0 rejected. |
| **Pass/Fail** | Each customer gets full quota independently |
| **Proves** | Per-customer isolation. A's traffic doesn't affect B. |

#### Scenario 5: Distributed Across Nodes
| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| **Input** | Customer A (100 RPM), send 100 requests distributed across Node 1, 2, 3 (round-robin or random) |
| **Expected** | Exactly 100 accepted total across all nodes, regardless of distribution |
| **Pass/Fail** | total_accepted == 100 |
| **Proves** | Distributed rate limiting is genuinely shared. Not per-node counters. |

#### Scenario 6: Concurrent Requests at Boundary
| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| **Input** | Customer A (100 RPM), send 150 requests concurrently across all nodes |
| **Expected** | Exactly 100 accepted, 50 rejected |
| **Pass/Fail** | accepted == 100, rejected == 50 |
| **Proves** | No race conditions at boundary. Atomicity works under concurrency. |

#### Scenario 7: Window Reset
| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| **Input** | Customer A (100 RPM). Send 100 (fill quota). Wait for window reset. Send 50 more. |
| **Expected** | First batch: 100 accepted. After reset: 50 accepted. |
| **Pass/Fail** | accepted_1 == 100, accepted_2 == 50 |
| **Proves** | Window resets correctly. Budget is replenished. |
| **Limitation** | ⚠️ Timing-sensitive: must wait for actual window boundary. |

#### Scenario 8: 429 + Retry-After
| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| **Input** | Customer A (100 RPM). Send 101 requests. Inspect the 429 response. |
| **Expected** | 101st request: status 429, `Retry-After` header present, value is seconds until next window, value is between 1 and 60. |
| **Pass/Fail** | Status == 429, Retry-After is valid integer in [1, 60] |
| **Proves** | Correct 429 semantics. Useful Retry-After value. |

### Harness Output Format

```
╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
║                    RelayAPI Rate Limiter — Load Harness Report                   ║
╠══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣

 Scenario 1: Below Quota
 ─────────────────────────
  Customer:   customer-1    Quota: 100 RPM
  Sent: 50    Accepted: 50    Rejected: 0
  Expected:   50 accepted, 0 rejected
  Result:     ✅ PASS

 Scenario 2: Exactly at Quota
 ─────────────────────────────
  Customer:   customer-1    Quota: 100 RPM
  Sent: 100   Accepted: 100   Rejected: 0
  Expected:   100 accepted, 0 rejected
  Result:     ✅ PASS

 ...

╠══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
║  SUMMARY: 8/8 scenarios passed                                                  ║
╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
```

### What the Harness Proves vs. Does NOT Prove

| Proves | Does NOT Prove |
|--------|----------------|
| Correct allow/reject at boundary | Behavior under sustained production load (thousands of RPM) |
| Customer isolation | Performance under memory pressure |
| Distributed correctness across nodes | Behavior with network partitions |
| Atomic concurrent handling | Long-term stability (hours/days) |
| Window reset works | Behavior under Redis failover |
| 429 + Retry-After format | Client retry correctness |
| No off-by-one at quota edge | Clock skew impact across real machines |
